claim: CloudWatch cross-account observability lets you monitor and troubleshoot applications that span multiple accounts within a Region.
q: Which CloudWatch feature lets one account monitor applications that span several accounts?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Unified-Cross-Account
With Amazon CloudWatch cross-account observability, you can monitor and troubleshoot applications that span multiple accounts within a Region.

claim: A monitoring account is a central AWS account that can view and interact with observability data generated from source accounts; a source account is an individual AWS account that generates observability data for the resources in it.
q: What are a monitoring account and a source account in CloudWatch cross-account observability?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Unified-Cross-Account

A monitoring account is a central AWS account that can view and interact with observability data generated from source accounts. A source account is an individual AWS account that generates observability data for the resources that reside in it.

claim: A sink is a resource that represents an attachment point in a monitoring account; source accounts link to the sink to share observability data, and each account can have one sink per Region.
q: What is a sink in CloudWatch cross-account observability?
v: an attachment point in a monitoring account
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Unified-Cross-Account
A *sink* is a resource that represents an attachment point in a monitoring account. Source accounts can link to the sink to share observability data. Each account can have one sink per Region.

claim: An observability link represents the link between a source account and a monitoring account, and links are managed by the source account; to remove a link, do so from the source account.
q: Which account manages and removes an observability link?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Unified-Cross-Account
An *observability link* is a resource that represents the link established between a source account and a monitoring account. Links are managed by the source account.
docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Unified-Cross-Account
To remove a link between accounts, do so from the source account.

claim: A source account can share all metric namespaces or a subset of namespaces, and all log groups or a subset of log groups, with the monitoring account.
q: What can a source account share with a monitoring account, and can it share only part of it?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Unified-Cross-Account
Metrics in Amazon CloudWatch. You can choose to share the metrics from all namespaces with the monitoring account, or filter to a subset of namespaces.
docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Unified-Cross-Account
Log groups in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. You can choose to share all log groups with the monitoring account, or filter to a subset of log groups.

claim: AWS recommends using AWS Organizations to link source accounts so that new accounts created later in the organization are automatically onboarded to cross-account observability as source accounts.
q: How do you onboard new accounts automatically as CloudWatch source accounts?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Unified-Cross-Account
We recommend that you use Organizations so that new AWS accounts created later in the organization are automatically onboarded to cross-account observability as source accounts.

claim: Cross-account observability in CloudWatch has no extra cost for logs and metrics or for Application Signals, and the first trace copy is free.
q: Does CloudWatch cross-account observability cost extra for shared logs and metrics?
v: no extra cost for logs and metrics
the first trace copy is free
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Unified-Cross-Account
Cross-account observability in CloudWatch comes with no extra cost for logs and metrics, Application Signals, and the first trace copy is free.

claim: If the source account selects more telemetry types than the monitoring account, link creation fails and nothing is shared; if the monitoring account selects more, the accounts are linked and only the types selected in both are shared.
q: What happens if a source account shares more telemetry types than the monitoring account accepts?
v: link creation fails and nothing is shared
selected in both accounts are shared
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Unified-Cross-Account
If there are more telemetry types selected in the *source account* than in the monitoring account, the link creation fails and nothing is shared.
docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Unified-Cross-Account
If there are more telemetry types selected in the *monitoring account* than in the source account, the accounts are linked. Only the data types that are selected in both accounts are shared.

claim: CloudWatch cross-account observability, the cross-account cross-Region console and cross-account cross-Region centralization are complementary and can be used independently or together; AWS recommends cross-account observability for the richest experience within a Region for metrics, logs and traces.
q: Which CloudWatch multi-account feature does AWS recommend within one Region?
v: We recommend that you use CloudWatch cross-account observability
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Cross-Account-Methods
These features are complementary to each other and can be used independently or together.
docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Cross-Account-Methods
We recommend that you use CloudWatch cross-account observability for the richest cross-account observability and discovery experience within a Region for your metrics, logs, and traces.

claim: The cross-account cross-Region CloudWatch console lets you view the dashboards, metrics and alarms consoles of other accounts across Regions by toggling between accounts.
q: Which CloudWatch feature lets you switch between accounts and Regions in the console?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Cross-Account-Methods

Cross-account cross-Region CloudWatch console– delivers a console experience that allows you to view dashboards, metrics, and alarms consoles of other accounts across Regions by toggling between accounts.

claim: CloudWatch Logs data centralization works with AWS Organizations: you define centralization rules that automatically replicate log data from multiple accounts and Regions into a centralized account within your organization.
q: How can CloudWatch Logs from many accounts and Regions be copied into one central account?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CloudWatchLogs_Centralization

Amazon CloudWatch Logs data centralization works with AWS Organizations to collect log data from multiple member accounts into one data repository using cross-account and cross-region centralization rules. You define the rules that automatically replicate log data from multiple accounts and AWS Regions into a centralized account within your organization.

claim: CloudWatch Logs centralization only processes new log data that arrives in source accounts after you create the centralization rule; historical log data is not centralized.
q: Does log centralization copy log data that existed before the rule was created?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CloudWatchLogs_Centralization

The CloudWatch Logs centralization feature only processes new log data that arrives in source accounts after you create the centralization rule. Historical log data (logs that existed before rule creation) is not centralized.

claim: Centralization rules are managed by the AWS Organizations management account or a delegated administrator.
q: Which account creates CloudWatch Logs centralization rules?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CloudWatchLogs_Centralization
Centralization rules are managed by the AWS Organizations management account or delegated administrator.

claim: CloudWatch Metrics centralization automatically centralizes metrics from multiple source accounts and Regions into a single destination account within your AWS Organizations organization, using rules that control what gets centralized.
q: How can CloudWatch metrics from many accounts and Regions be centralized?
v: You define rules to control what gets centralized
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatchMetrics_Centralization

Amazon CloudWatch Metrics centralization automatically centralizes metrics from multiple source accounts and Regions into a single destination account within your AWS Organizations organization. You define rules to control what gets centralized, enabling unified monitoring, alarming, and analysis across your entire AWS infrastructure.

claim: CloudWatch Logs lets you centralize the logs from all your systems, applications and AWS services in a single, highly scalable service, where you can view, search and filter them and archive them securely.
q: What is Amazon CloudWatch Logs used for?
v: centralize the logs from all of your systems
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/WhatIsCloudWatchLogs

CloudWatch Logs enables you to centralize the logs from all of your systems, applications, and AWS services that you use, in a single, highly scalable service. You can then easily view them, search them for specific error codes or patterns, filter them based on specific fields, or archive them securely for future analysis.

claim: By default CloudWatch Logs keeps logs indefinitely and they never expire; you can adjust the retention policy for each log group, keeping indefinite retention or choosing a period between 10 years and one day.
q: How long does CloudWatch Logs keep log data by default, and where is retention set?
v: retention policy for each log group
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/WhatIsCloudWatchLogs

By default, logs are kept indefinitely and never expire. You can adjust the retention policy for each log group, keeping the indefinite retention, or choosing a retention period between 10 years and one day.

claim: Retention settings are assigned to log groups and apply to their log streams; log events that pass the retention period expire and are deleted automatically.
q: What happens to log events after the retention period?
v: Expired log events get deleted automatically
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CloudWatchLogsConcepts

Retention settings can be used to specify how long log events are kept in CloudWatch Logs. Expired log events get deleted automatically. Just like metric filters, retention settings are also assigned to log groups, and the retention assigned to a log group is applied to their log streams.

claim: A log event is a record of activity with a timestamp and a raw message; a log stream is a log events that share the same source; a log group is a group of log streams that share the same retention, monitoring and access control settings.
q: How are log events, log streams and log groups related in CloudWatch Logs?
v: log events that share the same source
same retention, monitoring, and access control settings
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CloudWatchLogsConcepts
A log stream is a sequence of log events that share the same source.
docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CloudWatchLogsConcepts
Log groups define groups of log streams that share the same retention, monitoring, and access control settings. Each log stream has to belong to one log group.

claim: CloudWatch Logs has two log classes: Standard, a full-featured option for logs that need real-time monitoring or frequent access, and Infrequent Access, a lower-cost option with lower ingestion charges that supports a subset of the Standard class capabilities.
q: What are the two CloudWatch Logs log classes?
v: Infrequent Access log class incur lower ingestion charges
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/WhatIsCloudWatchLogs

CloudWatch Logs supports two *log classes*. Log groups in the *CloudWatch Logs Standard log class* support all CloudWatch Logs features. Log groups in the *CloudWatch Logs Infrequent Access log class* incur lower ingestion charges and support a subset of the Standard class capabilities.

claim: After a log group is created, its log class cannot be changed.
q: Can you change a log group from Standard to Infrequent Access later?
v: its log class can't be changed
After a log group is created
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CloudWatch_Logs_Log_Classes
After a log group is created, its log class can't be changed.

claim: For charges, the Standard and Infrequent Access log classes differ in ingestion costs only; storage charges and CloudWatch Logs Insights charges are the same in each class.
q: Which charges differ between the Standard and Infrequent Access log classes?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CloudWatch_Logs_Log_Classes
For charges, the Standard and Infrequent Access log classes differ in ingestion costs only. Storage charges and CloudWatch Logs Insights charges are the same in each log class.

claim: Subscription filters and Live Tail are supported only for log groups in the Standard log class, not for Infrequent Access.
q: Which features need the Standard log class instead of Infrequent Access?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/Subscriptions
Subscriptions are supported only for log groups in the Standard log class.
docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CloudWatchLogs_LiveTail
Live Tail is supported only for log groups in the Standard log class.
